findings.title: Pin and verify the downloaded installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This build fetches whatever content the mutable install.sh URL serves at build time and pipes it directly to sh. A compromised endpoint, DNS/TLS trust issue, or ordinary upstream script change can execute arbitrary code in the image build and produce different artifacts from the same source revision.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: This newly downloads and executes whatever example.com serves at build time, without a version pin or integrity check. A changed or compromised response executes as root during the image build and can alter the produced image.

findings.title: Propagate installer download failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The pipeline reports sh's exit status. If curl fails before writing input, sh can receive an empty script and exit successfully, allowing the image build to complete without the required installation.

findings.title: Pin and verify the installer before executing it
findings.whyItBreaks: Every image build downloads and executes whatever bytes this URL serves. A compromised, replaced, or intercepted response can run arbitrary commands in the build environment and alter the produced image; the URL and content have no version or checksum pin.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in the public helper
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ErrMissing for an absent key, but this exported API discards that error and returns "". Callers cannot distinguish a missing key from a present key whose value is legitimately empty.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported helper explicitly discards Load's ErrMissing return and emits "" for both an absent key and a present key with an empty value. External callers using this API therefore cannot handle a failed load distinctly from valid data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors in LoadOrDefault
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported wrapper discards Load's ErrMissing and returns "". External callers cannot distinguish an absent key from a key explicitly stored with an empty value.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Each result send now runs in an untracked goroutine, so Run can return while sends are pending. A caller that closes results after Run returns can trigger a panic, and callers can no longer rely on all results being sent at return.

findings.title: Wait for result sends before returning from Run
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed goroutines let Run return before any result send completes. A caller that treats Run's return as completion can close results afterward, causing a send-on-closed-channel panic; sends may also remain blocked indefinitely when unread.

findings.title: Preserve Run's completion boundary before returning
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, Run returned only after every result had been sent. The new goroutines allow Run to return while sends are still pending, so a caller that closes its caller-owned results channel after Run returns can cause a "send on closed channel" panic.

findings.title: Require admin status before deleting a record
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `||` predicate returns true when `isAdmin` is false but the session tenant matches the record tenant, bypassing the prior admin requirement for destructive record deletion.

findings.title: Require tenant-matched administrators for record deletion
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `||` grants deletion to a non-admin in the record's tenant or to an admin from another tenant. The prior predicate required both conditions.

findings.title: Keep tenant isolation in the delete authorization check
findings.whyItBreaks: Using || authorizes an admin from tenant A to delete a record belonging to tenant B. It also authorizes any non-admin user in the record's tenant, whereas the previous policy required both admin status and tenant ownership.

findings.title: Do not overwrite corrupt settings when changing font size
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed catch at lines 14-15 converts malformed or schema-invalid persisted settings into defaults. updateFontSize at src/settings.ts:20 then changes and saves that fallback, overwriting storage instead of preserving the parse failure.

findings.title: Preserve parse errors instead of silently resetting settings
findings.whyItBreaks: Malformed or schema-invalid saved settings previously raised an error; they now become a valid default Settings value. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and saves it, permanently replacing the user's existing theme and other recoverable settings without exposing the corruption.

findings.title: Preserve parse failures instead of persisting default settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The new catch turns invalid JSON or invalid settings fields into DEFAULTS. updateFontSize then changes that fallback and calls save at src/settings.ts:22, overwriting malformed or incompatible stored settings rather than preserving the prior error behavior.

findings.title: Return artifacts for the reported commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` remains the commit resolved for the caller-provided branch, but the changed return now fetches `artifacts` from `verified`. Reports for a branch other than `verified` therefore contain internally inconsistent build data.

findings.title: Fetch artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: builtFrom remains the commit resolved from the caller-supplied branch, but artifacts are fetched from the separate "verified" ref. A report for branch A can therefore claim it was built from A while listing artifacts from verified.

findings.title: Load artifacts from the reported branch commit
findings.whyItBreaks: `builtFrom` remains `build.ref(branch)`, but `artifacts` are now read from `build.ref("verified")`. A report for a branch whose ref differs from `verified` associates verified-branch artifacts with the requested branch commit.

findings.title: Apply the requested positive limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, this returns every reversed entry instead of at most `limit`. Consequently, renderFeed's call with 20 iterates over all entries and extends its nominal 20-slot array beyond 20 items.

findings.title: Restore the limit when returning sorted entries
findings.whyItBreaks: For any positive limit, this returns every entry rather than at most limit entries. `renderFeed` passes 20 at src/feed.ts:9; with 21 inputs, its loop assigns index 20 and returns 21 entries.

findings.title: Restore the requested entry limit
findings.whyItBreaks: For every positive limit, the function now returns every entry rather than at most `limit`. `renderFeed` passes 20 and writes every returned entry into its output array, expanding it beyond 20 when more entries are supplied.

findings.title: Count only emitted manifest rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed filter omits stale entries from the rendered rows, but the header still receives entries.length. The emitted manifest can therefore declare an entry count larger than the number of data rows it contains.

findings.title: Keep entry-count aligned with emitted rows
findings.whyItBreaks: For input containing stale entries, rows contains only live entries but the header still uses entries.length, so `# entry-count` exceeds the number of emitted manifest rows. Consumers receive internally inconsistent manifest metadata.

findings.title: Count only rows that are emitted
findings.whyItBreaks: When any entry is stale, its row is removed but `# entry-count` is still calculated from `entries.length`. The manifest therefore advertises more entries than it contains, breaking consumers that use the header to validate or parse the row set.

findings.title: Restore the exported legacy ID formatter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing exported FormatLegacyID is a source-breaking API change: downstream callers producing LEG-formatted IDs will no longer compile and no replacement API is provided.

findings.title: Preserve the exported legacy-ID formatter or document a breaking migration
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed hunk deletes the exported FormatLegacyID symbol. Downstream packages that call it will fail to compile when upgrading; no replacement is provided.

findings.title: Preserve the exported shippingQuote compatibility shim
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported shippingQuote function is a source and runtime compatibility break for consumers importing it from this module.

findings.title: Preserve the shippingQuote export
findings.whyItBreaks: Consumers importing shippingQuote from src/orders now fail to compile because this changed module no longer exports it. Adding quoteShipping in a new module does not preserve the prior module API.

findings.title: Restore execute's successful transformation
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the public execute(input) function now throws "always fails" and cannot return a result; the prior implementation returned input.toUpperCase().

findings.title: Restore execute's string-returning behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported signature promises a string result, but every invocation now throws. This regresses the prior behavior of returning input.toUpperCase() and breaks callers expecting a result.

findings.title: Restore execute's string result
findings.whyItBreaks: Every call to the exported execute(input): string function now throws, so callers cannot obtain the prior uppercase result or any string result at all.

findings.title: Preserve read-only handling for active viewers
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer with fewer than five attempts, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected". The existing viewer-specific "read-only" result is therefore unreachable.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only viewer path
findings.whyItBreaks: The new viewer rejection makes active viewers return "rejected" before handle can reach its existing "read-only" branch at src/handler.ts:24.

findings.title: Preserve viewers' read-only handling
findings.whyItBreaks: For an active viewer below the attempt limit, isEligible now returns false, so handle returns "rejected" at src/handler.ts:24. The following branch explicitly classifies viewers as "read-only", and is now unreachable.

findings.title: Split payment eligibility from draft saving
findings.whyItBreaks: For a draft with payment="missing", canProceed now returns false, so saveDraft returns "blocked" instead of "saved".

findings.title: Read files from the reported channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: When a channel head differs from stable, the returned Snapshot.commit is the channel head but Snapshot.files is read from stable. Consumers therefore receive files from a different revision than the reported snapshot.

findings.title: Read files from the snapshot commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The returned Snapshot sets `commit` to the requested channel head but reads `files` from `stable`. When those refs differ, callers receive internally inconsistent snapshot metadata and contents.

findings.title: Read snapshot files from the requested channel head
findings.whyItBreaks: publishSnapshot records repo.headCommit(channel) in Snapshot.commit but now passes repo.headCommit("stable") to filesAt. For any non-stable channel, the returned snapshot describes two different revisions.

findings.title: Honor the limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build(prefix, limit=10)` newly exposes a caller-controlled result cap, but the body still assigns `max_count = 10`. Thus `build("x", 3)` returns ten entries rather than three.

findings.title: Honor the newly exposed limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: `build("item", 3)` still returns ten items because the implementation always assigns `max_count = 10`. The new public parameter promises a caller-observable result cap but has no effect.

findings.title: Honor the build limit parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Calling build("x", limit=1) still returns 10 items because max_count remains hard-coded to 10. The new public parameter promises a caller-visible output cap but has no effect.

findings.title: Reject non-positive inputs in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1 despite its new public name promising a positive integer; the changed in-file consumer at src/validators.py:6 then produces a negative charge.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int(-1) and parse_positive_int(0) return valid integers despite its new positive-integer name. charge consequently returns negative or zero cents for those inputs.

findings.title: Reject non-positive values in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int('-1') returns -1 and parse_positive_int('0') returns 0, contradicting the new positive-value contract. charge() consequently returns negative or zero cents.

findings.title: Preserve the caller DataFrame instead of mutating it
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed assignment mutates the caller-owned DataFrame and returns the same object. The base implementation copied df before applying mappings, so callers retaining df now unexpectedly observe modified values.

findings.title: Preserve the input DataFrame
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this change, apply_values modified a copy and left df unchanged. It now writes directly through df.loc, so callers that reuse the input DataFrame after deriving transformed output observe their source data silently altered.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1`, while zero and invalid input return `0`; this newly named public API therefore violates its positive-value contract. The changed in-repo consumer, `charge` at `src/parse.rs:6`, propagates those values into its returned amount.

findings.title: Enforce positivity in parse_positive_int
findings.whyItBreaks: parse_positive_int("-1") returns -1 and parse_positive_int("0") returns 0, contradicting the newly introduced positive-integer contract. Its in-file consumer charge consequently permits negative or zero charges.

findings.title: Enforce the positive-integer contract
findings.whyItBreaks: `parse_positive_int("-1")` returns `-1`, despite its public name promising a positive integer. Its caller then computes `charge("-1")` as `-100`, allowing a negative charge.

findings.title: Borrow items in the debug call
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and consumes the `Vec<String>` by value. Line 3 subsequently borrows `items` for `len()`, producing Rust error E0382 (use of moved value) and preventing the crate from compiling.

findings.title: Borrow items when logging
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items);` moves and drops the owned `Vec<String>`, so the subsequent `items.len()` uses a moved value and produces Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Avoid moving `items` into the debug macro
findings.whyItBreaks: `dbg!(items)` evaluates and consumes the `Vec<String>` by value. `items.len()` on line 3 then attempts to borrow the moved value, producing Rust error E0382.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the returned revision
findings.whyItBreaks: If `pinnedTag` resolves differently from `latest`, `changedPaths` describes a different revision than `fromRevision`. The returned `Changeset` therefore cannot be replayed against its stated base revision.

findings.title: Compute changed paths from the advertised base revision
findings.whyItBreaks: When pinnedTag resolves to a revision different from latest, changedPaths is computed against latest but the Changeset advertises fromRevision as the pinned revision. Consumers replaying these paths atop fromRevision receive a delta for the wrong base revision.

findings.title: Compute paths from the revision reported in fromRevision
findings.whyItBreaks: The public Changeset contract says changedPaths were computed against fromRevision, but this change resolves `latest` and passes it to readChangedPaths while returning the pinned revision as fromRevision. Callers replaying paths against fromRevision can receive paths for a different base revision.

findings.title: Update the query for the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` no longer exists, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`; databases applying migration 0002 will reject that query with a missing-column error.

findings.title: Update queries for the renamed email column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, `users.email` is removed, but `src/query.sql:1` still executes `SELECT email FROM users`, which fails with a missing-column SQL error on upgraded databases when that query runs.

findings.title: Update queries to use the renamed column
findings.whyItBreaks: After this migration, users.email no longer exists, but src/query.sql still executes SELECT email FROM users. Any consumer of that query fails with an unknown/no-such column error after upgrading.

findings.title: Restore environment-sourced billing credentials
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed line hard-codes a billing key, so every deployment ignores BILLING_API_KEY and authenticates with the source-controlled credential. This exposes the credential to repository readers and prevents per-environment configuration or normal credential rotation.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing API key
findings.whyItBreaks: The literal bk_live_... credential is committed to the repository, exposing billing API access to anyone who can read the source or its history. It also bypasses the deployment-specific BILLING_API_KEY configuration.

findings.title: Remove the committed live billing credential
findings.whyItBreaks: Every makeClient() call now uses the committed bk_live key instead of BILLING_API_KEY. The credential is exposed to everyone with repository access and deployed environments can no longer select or rotate their own billing credential.

findings.title: Allow admins to purge archived projects
findings.whyItBreaks: For an admin with an archived project, this returns "forbidden" before deletion. The base behavior purged exactly that combination, so the authorized purge workflow is now blocked.

findings.title: Restore the admin authorization condition
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `if (user.isAdmin) return "forbidden"` rejects admins. A non-admin with an archived project passes both guards, reaches `db.delete(project.id)`, and receives "purged", enabling an unauthorized destructive action.

findings.title: Restore the admin authorization check before purging
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed guards return "forbidden" for every admin, while a non-admin with an archived project reaches `db.delete(project.id)`. This permits unauthorized destructive deletion of archived projects.

findings.title: Restore the missing-config fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: For a nonexistent path, load_settings returns None at app/config.py:6-7. The changed startup path then evaluates settings["workers"] at line 14, raising TypeError instead of preserving the prior default worker count.

findings.title: Preserve missing-file defaults in startup
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None for a nonexistent path (app/config.py:6-7). Removing the fallback means startup now evaluates None["workers"] and raises TypeError instead of starting with the prior one-worker default.

findings.title: Restore the missing-settings fallback
findings.whyItBreaks: load_settings returns None when path does not exist (app/config.py:6-7). startup now immediately subscripts that None value, raising TypeError instead of preserving the previous default of one worker.

findings.title: Propagate gateway submission failures
findings.whyItBreaks: When Gateway.Submit returns an error, exported Charge logs it and returns nil. Callers therefore cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one.

findings.title: Propagate failed gateway submissions
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed error branch logs a Gateway.Submit failure but then falls through to `return nil`. Since Charge is exported, callers—including external consumers—cannot distinguish a failed charge from a successful one and may mark an unpaid order as paid.

findings.title: Propagate gateway failures from Charge
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Charge API now logs a Gateway.Submit failure and returns nil, so callers cannot distinguish a failed charge from a completed one.

findings.title: Keep tenant ID in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After tenant A fetches setting `name`, the cache stores it as `settings:name`. A later `settingsFor(tenantB, name, store)` returns that cached value at line 14 without calling `store.fetch(tenantB, name)`, leaking/cross-applying tenant A's configuration.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping to cache keys
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor fetches with tenantId, but the changed cache key uses only name. Once one tenant caches a setting, another tenant requesting the same name receives that cached value before its own store.fetch call.

findings.title: Include tenantId in the settings cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: settingsFor fetches values using tenantId, but cacheKey now uses only name. After tenant A reads a setting, tenant B reading the same name receives tenant A's cached value without calling store.fetch.

findings.title: Serialize reservations for each SKU before persisting
findings.whyItBreaks: Two concurrent calls can both read stock=1, both pass the availability guard, then await save(0). Both return true even though only one item existed, producing an oversold reservation.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations before persisting stock
findings.whyItBreaks: The new await yields after concurrent calls have read the same stock value. With stock=1, two reserve calls can both save remaining=0 and both return true, granting two reservations for one item.

findings.title: Serialize concurrent reservations for the same SKU
findings.whyItBreaks: The new await yields before local stock is decremented. With one unit in stock, two concurrent reserve calls can both read remaining=1, both save 0, and both return true.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1,000 ms, but retry() still multiplies it by 1,000 at src/jobs/retry.ts:12. Its first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1 second.

findings.title: Keep retry delays in milliseconds
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff(0) now returns 1000 milliseconds, but retry still passes backoff(a) * 1000 to sleep. The first retry therefore waits 1,000,000 ms instead of 1 second; capped retries wait over 8 hours.

findings.title: Update retry to consume millisecond backoff values
findings.whyItBreaks: backoff() now returns milliseconds, but retry() still multiplies it by 1,000 before passing it to sleep(). The first retry changes from 1,000 ms to 1,000,000 ms, and the capped retry delay changes from 30 seconds to over 8 hours.

findings.title: Propagate the file-close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The new deferred Close discards its error. When Flush succeeds but Close reports an I/O failure, the exported Save function now returns nil; the base implementation returned that Close error.

findings.title: Propagate the deferred close error
findings.whyItBreaks: The previous implementation returned f.Close() errors after a successful flush. The new deferred Close return value is discarded, so callers of exported Save cannot distinguish a successful persisted file from a close failure.

findings.title: Propagate file-close failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The new deferred f.Close() discards its error. Previously, a successful Flush followed by a failing Close was returned to Save's caller; now Save returns nil, allowing callers to treat an incompletely committed write as successful.

findings.title: Include the end-of-page row in page_window
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed loop uses range(start, end - 1) even though _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) bounds. This omits index end - 1 from every non-empty page; a page_size of 1 renders no rows.

findings.title: Include the page end position when collecting rows
findings.whyItBreaks: _window_bounds returns half-open [start, end) bounds, but the changed loop uses range(start, end - 1). This omits the last row of every page and makes one-row pages empty. render_page (lib/pagination.py:40) and summarize (lib/pagination.py:52) expose the truncated output.

findings.title: Return the final row of each page
findings.whyItBreaks: The bounds are documented as half-open, but `range(start, end - 1)` excludes index `end - 1`. A one-row page returns no rows, and `render_page`/`summarize` consequently omit each page's last row.

findings.title: Return entries only while their TTL is valid
findings.whyItBreaks: A freshly stored entry has age below ttlMs, so the changed condition deletes it and returns null. After expiry, the cache returns the stale value.

findings.title: Remove every completed job without mutating the input
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forward forEach iteration shifts the next job into the current index, which forEach skips. For `[done, done]`, one completed job remains; the function also now mutates its input.

findings.title: Restore the non-expired TTL condition
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has an age near zero, so it fails `age > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned instead of evicted.

findings.title: Avoid splicing while iterating completed jobs
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing an element shifts the next job into the current index, but `forEach` then advances to the next index. Two consecutive completed jobs therefore leave the second completed job in the returned array.

findings.title: Preserve pruneDone's non-mutating behavior
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior exported function returned a filtered copy and left the caller's array unchanged. The new implementation splices the supplied array, so callers that retain it observe their job list unexpectedly losing completed entries.

findings.title: Return entries only before their TTL expires
findings.whyItBreaks: A newly stored entry has age 0, so it fails `0 > ttlMs`, is deleted, and returns null. Conversely, expired entries are returned indefinitely.

findings.title: Remove every completed job without skipping adjacent entries
findings.whyItBreaks: Splicing during forward `forEach` shifts the next job into the removed index, but `forEach` advances to the following index. For `[done, done]`, the second completed job remains in the returned queue.

findings.title: Restore numeric comparison when ranking scores
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator coerces scores to strings. For players ordered as score 9 then 100 with n=1, sorting and reversing produces [9, 100], so topPlayers uses cutoff 9 and returns the 9-point input player instead of the 100-point player.

findings.title: Restore numeric score ordering
findings.whyItBreaks: Array#sort without a comparator orders numbers as strings. For players scored 2 and 10 with n=1, rankScores returns [2, 10], so topPlayers sets a cutoff of 2 and returns the first input player rather than the highest scorer.

findings.title: Restore numeric sorting for leaderboard scores
findings.whyItBreaks: Array.sort() without a comparator sorts numbers as strings. For scores [9, 100, 8] and n=1, rankScores produces [9, 8, 100], making the cutoff 9; topPlayers then returns the first qualifying input player rather than the player with score 100.

findings.title: Restore constant-time HMAC signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed equality comparison may expose prefix-dependent verification timing. A valid signature permits handle() to invoke processor(payload).

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `==` comparison can return sooner for signatures with earlier mismatches, exposing an HMAC-digest timing signal to callers that can repeatedly submit webhook signatures. A valid inferred signature passes `verify` and reaches `processor(payload)`.

findings.title: Restore constant-time signature comparison
findings.whyItBreaks: Using == can return sooner for signatures with an earlier mismatch, leaking prefix-match timing. An attacker able to make repeated verification requests can use this signal to incrementally forge a valid webhook signature.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transfer transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction commits after `_record_ledger` at line 23. If either subsequent balance update fails, the ledger entry cannot roll back; if the credit update fails after the debit, balances are left unbalanced.

findings.title: Keep ledger and balance updates in one transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed code exits `db.transaction()` after inserting the ledger row, then performs both balance updates outside it. If either update raises, the ledger entry has already committed and no longer rolls back with the failed transfer.

findings.title: Keep balance updates inside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: The transaction ends before line 24. If either balance update raises, the ledger insert has already committed; if the second update raises, the debit may also remain applied without its matching credit.

findings.title: Preserve UTC when deriving the billing-day key
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return expression uses local-time getters. For the same instant, a non-UTC process can now emit a different key; e.g. 2026-08-23T16:30:00Z is 2026-08-24 in Asia/Taipei rather than 2026-08-23. That assigns billing-boundary events to the wrong day.

findings.title: Keep billing-day keys in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return at src/billing/day.ts:4 replaces UTC getters with host-local getters. For 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z, a process in America/Los_Angeles now emits 2025-12-31 rather than the prior 2026-01-01, causing identical instants to receive different billing keys across deployment timezones.

findings.title: Keep billing-day calculation in UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed return expression uses local-time components rather than the previous UTC components. At 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z on an America/Los_Angeles host, it returns 2025-12-31 instead of 2026-01-01, assigning billing records to a different day based on server timezone.

findings.title: Keep tenant identity in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: A cached profile for tenant A/account X is returned for tenant B/account X because the changed key uses only `account` and the cache-hit branch returns it without calling `fetchProfile`. This exposes tenant-A profile data across tenant boundaries.

findings.title: Restore tenant isolation in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After a lookup for tenant A and account X caches its Profile, a lookup for tenant B and the same account X hits that entry and returns tenant A's profile without calling fetchProfile. This breaks tenant isolation and can disclose another tenant's profile data.

findings.title: Restore tenant scoping in the profile cache key
findings.whyItBreaks: After reading tenant A's account `x`, reading tenant B's account `x` returns the cached Profile for tenant A and never calls `fetchProfile` for tenant B. The Profile value includes `tenant`, exposing incorrect cross-tenant profile data.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `load` API previously propagated `Error("missing: <key>")`; this catch now returns `""`, which is indistinguishable from a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking successful results containing empty strings instead of reporting that a requested key is absent.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key errors from load
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported `load` API now returns `""` when a key is absent, conflating a missing value with a legitimately stored empty string. `loadAll` consequently returns partial-looking successful results instead of surfacing the missing key.

findings.title: Preserve missing-key failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The new empty catch converts the deliberately thrown missing-key error into "". Because empty strings are valid stored values, callers of exported load cannot distinguish absent data from stored empty data; loadAll (src/store.ts:12) likewise returns a successful array.

findings.title: Preserve the existing Config timeout field for upgrades
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Config contract removes timeoutMs and adds required retries and timeout. Existing TypeScript callers passing { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer compile; JavaScript callers retain no value for config.timeout, making the deadline NaN and disabling deadline enforcement.

findings.title: Return the final failure from retryBackground
findings.whyItBreaks: When every invocation of fn throws, this exported function catches each error and returns normally after the loop, exactly as it would after success. Callers cannot distinguish exhausted retries from completed background work.

findings.title: Expose retryBackground exhaustion as a failure
findings.whyItBreaks: When every invocation throws, the catch consumes the final error and the exported function returns void, exactly like successful completion. Callers cannot distinguish a completed background retry from one where no attempt succeeded.

findings.title: Preserve compatibility for existing Config callers
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported Config replaces required timeoutMs with required retries and timeout. Existing TypeScript callers supplying { maxAttempts, timeoutMs } no longer type-check. Existing JavaScript callers pass undefined for timeout, producing a NaN deadline and disabling the timeout comparison.

findings.title: Make retryBackground actually run in the background
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground invokes fn inline in a synchronous loop and does not queue, defer, or await background work. Callers of this exported API block until attempts finish, despite its background-execution contract.

findings.title: Expose failure after background retries are exhausted
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty catch discards every callback exception, and the exported function returns void on both success and exhausted failure. Consumers therefore cannot distinguish completed work from permanent failure.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps` now publicly accepts `number`, but `number` has no `length` property. TypeScript rejects this access, and numeric values would produce `len=undefined` if emitted despite type errors.

findings.title: Handle numeric Field values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: `FieldProps.value` now accepts `number`, but the changed label expression reads `value.length`. TypeScript rejects property access on the `string | number` union, blocking type-checked builds; numeric values would also produce `len=undefined` if emitted without type checking.

findings.title: Handle numeric values before reading length
findings.whyItBreaks: FieldProps now permits `value={42}`, but the changed implementation reads `value.length`; numbers have no `length`. This is a TypeScript error, and unchecked transpiled builds produce `len=undefined` for valid numeric inputs.

score.error: critic produced no summary or checked list (likely malformed output)

findings.title: Restore the git output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit 64 MiB maxBuffer restores Node's 1 MiB spawnSync default. The same helper captures the complete PR patch at line 140, so a diff larger than 1 MiB makes git fail and the review is reported as failed instead of being submitted.

findings.title: Restore the Git diff output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` now uses `spawnSync`'s default 1 MiB `maxBuffer`. Diffs exceeding it cause `git()` to throw, so `runGithub` reports the review as failed instead of reviewing the PR.

findings.title: Restore the Git output buffer limit
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults maxBuffer to 1 MiB. The same helper produces the full PR patch at line 140, so a PR with a diff over 1 MiB is terminated by spawnSync and the review fails instead of being posted.

findings.title: Preserve the read-only sandbox for review runs
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex launches a prompt-controlled Codex process with opts.repoPath as its working directory. Removing the explicit '-s read-only' argument means this review runner no longer enforces that the process is unable to modify the reviewed workspace; sandbox selection is left to the Codex CLI configuration/default.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only Codex sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` removes the per-invocation sandbox restriction before spawning Codex in `opts.repoPath`. The exported wrapper accepts a prompt and runs it in the target repository, so a configured or default writable Codex sandbox can alter the repository being reviewed.

findings.title: Restore the enforced read-only sandbox
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `-s read-only` makes this review wrapper inherit Codex's configured/default sandbox policy. A writable policy lets model-generated commands modify `opts.repoPath` during a review, whereas the previous invocation enforced the wrapper's read-only security boundary.

findings.title: Restore merge-base before generating the PR diff
findings.whyItBreaks: When `baseSha` is a newer base-branch commit that is not an ancestor of the PR checkout, `git diff baseSha HEAD` compares the two tips and includes base-only changes as reverse changes. This makes both the review patch and `changedPaths` include files outside the PR, affecting review context and inline-comment eligibility.

findings.title: Use the resolved PR head for review input
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checked-out HEAD, the patch and changed-file set are calculated from HEAD but the review and check are posted to headSha. The published result can therefore describe a different commit than the PR head.

findings.title: Diff against the configured head SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: When PR_HEAD_SHA differs from the checkout's HEAD, the changed lines compute patch and changedFiles from HEAD, while the bundle and submitted review use headSha. This can analyze one commit and attach its review to another.

findings.title: Preserve literal `$` content when injecting prompt data
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace treats a string replacement value as a replacement template. Valid patch, bundle, or candidate content containing `$&`, `$'`, or `$`` is expanded instead of inserted literally; for example, a patch containing `$&` injects the matched placeholder text rather than the source content. This makes the review and critic receive a corrupted bundle, findings payload, or patch.

findings.title: Preserve literal dollar sequences when interpolating prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace interprets replacement tokens such as `$&`, `$`` and `$'`. Bundle data, candidate findings, and raw patches can contain arbitrary source text, so those sequences are rewritten before `runCodex` receives the generated review or critic prompt, producing corrupted review context.

findings.title: Preserve literal content when injecting the review bundle
findings.whyItBreaks: String.replace interprets `$&`, `$`` and `$'` in a string replacement. A bundle field containing these sequences is changed while constructing `reviewPrompt`, so Codex receives corrupted bundle metadata or patch text.

findings.title: Preserve literal findings and patch text in the critic prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: Both changed String.replace calls interpret replacement tokens. Candidate findings or source diffs containing `$&`, `$`` or `$'` are altered while constructing `criticPrompt`, giving the critic incorrect findings or patch content.

findings.title: Keep the fallback review pinned to the reviewed SHA
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed fallback omits `commit_id`, so GitHub can associate that fallback review with the PR's current head rather than the SHA reviewed by this run. `runGithub` captures `headSha` before calling `review()` and passes it to `postReview`; a push during review can therefore cause a REQUEST_CHANGES or passing fallback review to apply to unreviewed code.

findings.title: Preserve the reviewed commit in the fallback request
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary review POST fails and execution enters this fallback, the removed `commit_id` means GitHub targets the PR's current head rather than `headSha`, which is the commit used to build and review the bundle. A push during that interval can therefore attach the verdict to an unreviewed revision.

findings.title: Keep the review bound to the reviewed commit
findings.whyItBreaks: When the primary request fails and a new commit is pushed while review() is running, this fallback omits commit_id. GitHub defaults the review to the PR's most recent commit, even though result and the check run were computed for headSha. An APPROVE can therefore be attached to an unreviewed commit.

findings.title: Keep malformed findings distinguishable from P1 bugs
findings.whyItBreaks: An input finding with an invalid severity previously raised an error; it now becomes an otherwise legitimate-looking P1 finding. Consumers cannot distinguish malformed review output from a real P1 bug, so invalid model output can be displayed, persisted, or acted on as a real finding.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of fabricating them
findings.whyItBreaks: Invalid severity, category, required text, and location fields no longer propagate validation errors. They are returned as ordinary Finding data with defaults such as P1, bug, an empty file, and line 0, so callers cannot distinguish malformed review output from a real finding.

findings.title: Preserve the exported lenient-mode parameter
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the exported strict parameter breaks TypeScript consumers calling normalizeReview(raw, false). JavaScript consumers may still pass false, but it is ignored and malformed entries are now normalized into fallback findings rather than filtered.

findings.title: Reject malformed findings instead of manufacturing defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: A malformed object such as `{}` is now converted into a returned finding with synthetic P1/bug metadata, an empty file, and line 0. `normalizeReview` returns this object at line 131, so invalid review output is indistinguishable from an actual finding.

findings.title: Preserve the exported tolerant normalization mode
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing `strict` from this exported function is source-incompatible for TypeScript callers that pass `false`. For JavaScript callers, `normalizeReview(raw, false)` no longer drops malformed object entries as before; it returns the default-filled findings produced by `normalizeFinding`.

findings.title: Restore explicit repository selection for manual dispatch
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so the changed gh pr view commands run before checkout at .github/workflows/review.yml:42. Removing -R leaves gh without an explicit repository to query, so ref resolution can fail and Checkout PR head receives no PR head SHA.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty and lines 38-39 run before actions/checkout. Removing -R "$REPO" leaves gh pr view without a guaranteed repository context, so it can fail to resolve the PR and emit empty head/base outputs; checkout then receives an invalid ref.

findings.title: Keep the explicit repository when resolving manual PR refs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, EVENT_HEAD is empty, so this branch runs before the first actions/checkout step. The workspace therefore has no checked-out repository from which gh pr view can infer a target; after removing -R, both PR-SHA lookups lack repository context and the checkout receives empty outputs.

findings.title: Preserve malformed review-output failures
findings.whyItBreaks: This exported parser now defaults missing or invalid required top-level fields to empty values, collapsing malformed model output into a successful empty review. Consumers can therefore treat failed review generation as a legitimate review with no findings or risks.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: A null or structurally invalid model response previously threw a malformed-review error; it now becomes an empty RawReview. Because normalizeReview is exported, callers cannot distinguish a failed/malformed review from a legitimate review with no findings or risks.

findings.title: Preserve malformed-review failures
findings.whyItBreaks: The exported normalizer now converts absent or wrongly typed required review fields into a valid empty review. Consumers can no longer distinguish malformed reviewer output from a legitimate clean review and may persist or report a false pass.

findings.title: Resolve the requested PR before manual dispatch checkout
findings.whyItBreaks: On workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so changed line 29 falls back to github.ref—the branch selected when dispatching—rather than the head of inputs.pr_number. The review invocation at .github/workflows/review.yml:47 still targets the supplied PR number, causing the tool to run from an unrelated checkout. The same event fields also leave PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA empty on manual dispatch.

findings.title: Resolve refs for workflow-dispatch reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent. The changed checkout expression therefore falls back to github.ref, the base fetch defaults to main, and lines 45-46 pass empty PR SHA values to the review command at .github/workflows/review.yml:47. The supplied pr_number is not used to resolve its requested PR's head or base.

findings.title: Restore PR-ref resolution for manual dispatches
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, the pull_request fields are absent. The changed checkout therefore uses github.ref (the branch or tag selected when dispatching), rather than the PR identified by pr_number; PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA are also empty. The review can consequently analyze and report against a revision unrelated to the requested PR.

findings.title: Restore the git diff output buffer
findings.whyItBreaks: `runLocal` obtains the entire patch with `git diff baseSha HEAD` at line 100. Without `maxBuffer`, Node's `spawnSync` default is 1 MiB; a larger diff terminates with a buffer error/status and this wrapper throws, so the reviewer cannot process otherwise valid large PRs. The previous 64 MiB limit explicitly supported these inputs.

findings.title: Preserve capacity for large Git diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `git()` helper now uses Node's default 1 MiB `spawnSync` buffer. `runLocal` obtains the complete patch through `git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd)` at `src/adapters/local.ts:98`, so diffs larger than that fail before a review can be produced.

findings.title: Restore a buffer large enough for review diffs
findings.whyItBreaks: Without maxBuffer, spawnSync uses Node’s 1 MiB default. The git diff call at src/adapters/local.ts:100 captures the entire patch, so a diff exceeding 1 MiB terminates with a buffer error and git() throws before runLocal can submit any review.

findings.title: Report review execution errors as failed checks
findings.whyItBreaks: The error handler now sends the named `Needlefish` check with conclusion `neutral` after `review()` or result posting throws. GitHub treats `neutral` as successful for required status checks, so a branch that requires this check can merge despite the review failing to execute.

findings.title: Keep review failures as failing check runs
findings.whyItBreaks: When review() or posting the review throws, this publishes the Needlefish check as neutral even though the process reports a review failure. Neutral check conclusions are non-failing, so a branch protection rule relying on the Needlefish check can treat an errored review as acceptable rather than blocking the PR.

findings.title: Keep review errors blocking
findings.whyItBreaks: GitHub treats a neutral required check as successful. If review(), review posting, or normal check posting throws, this catch path now publishes Needlefish as neutral even though the review did not run to completion, allowing a PR protected by this check to merge without the intended review gate.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer on a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed command executes src/cli.ts from the checked-out PR head while GH_TOKEN has pull-requests: write and checks: write. A same-repository PR can alter the reviewer to emit fabricated review results or use that token, bypassing the review gate. The prior workflow installed and executed a separate frankekn/needlefish@main checkout.

findings.title: Keep the reviewer checkout independent of the PR
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed command executes src/cli.ts from the checked-out same-repository PR head. A PR can alter that code or its install inputs, then use the available GH_TOKEN permissions (pull-requests: write and checks: write) to forge its own review result.

findings.title: Restore a checkout that contains the reviewer package
findings.whyItBreaks: HEAD contains only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json; it has no package.json or src/cli.ts. The changed install command therefore has no package manifest, and the subsequent changed invocation cannot resolve its CLI, so every review job fails before producing a review.

findings.title: Keep the review executable on a trusted revision
findings.whyItBreaks: The same-repository PR guard permits a PR head to be checked out, then its dependency install scripts and `src/cli.ts` are executed. The review command receives a token with `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`, allowing a PR to replace the reviewer or install behavior and alter its own review output or execute code on the self-hosted runner.

findings.title: Restore the checkout containing the CLI and package manifest
findings.whyItBreaks: This head contains only `.github/workflows/review.yml` and `.needlefish/answers.json`, with no `package.json` or `src/cli.ts`. `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` therefore cannot install the project, and the subsequent CLI path is absent.

findings.title: Restore canonical severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview accepts untyped raw output and passes each finding here. A valid case/whitespace variant such as severity: "p0" or " P2 " previously normalized to P0/P2, but now fails exact membership and is emitted as P3, causing real high-severity findings to be downgraded.

findings.title: Restore case-insensitive severity normalization
findings.whyItBreaks: A raw finding with severity " p1 " or "p1" previously normalized to "P1"; it now fails the exact-match check and is returned as "P3". This changes valid review findings into lower-priority findings when input casing or whitespace differs.

findings.title: Preserve canonicalization before validating severity
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeReview passes untyped parsed findings to normalizeFinding. The new exact-membership check rejects values such as "p0" or " P1 ", returning P3 instead. Before this diff, these values were trimmed and uppercased, so critical findings can now be silently reported at the lowest severity.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the `env` option at the changed spawn call makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. Codex receives the supplied prompt and runs in the supplied repository, so untrusted instructions can direct subprocesses to exfiltrate these credentials.

findings.title: Keep GitHub tokens out of the Codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit `env` option makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN. The invoked Codex process can read these credentials despite its read-only filesystem sandbox; its prompt is caller-controlled and may include untrusted repository content.

findings.title: Keep GitHub credentials out of the Codex child
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the explicit `env` option makes `spawnSync` inherit `process.env`, including `GH_TOKEN`, `GITHUB_TOKEN`, and `GITHUB_API_TOKEN`. The child receives the supplied prompt, so prompt-driven code can read or disclose those inherited credentials despite the read-only filesystem sandbox.

findings.title: Restore the fork guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted condition was the only restriction preventing fork-originated PRs from reaching this self-hosted job. The job checks out the fork's exact head SHA and then runs `pnpm install` plus `tsx src/cli.ts` from that checkout, so a fork can supply arbitrary install hooks or source code for execution on the runner.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard before running PR code
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job-level condition allows a pull request from a fork to check out its attacker-controlled head SHA, install its dependencies, and run its CLI on a self-hosted runner. A fork author can modify package scripts or the invoked source to compromise the runner and any credentials or network access available to it.

findings.title: Restore the same-repository guard on the self-hosted job
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing the job condition allows fork PRs to reach this self-hosted runner. The workflow checks out the fork-controlled PR SHA, installs its dependencies, and executes its `src/cli.ts`, allowing untrusted code to execute in the runner environment.

findings.title: Preserve zero-valued duration overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: The prior parser explicitly accepted 0. Now NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 falls back to 5000, delaying SIGKILL by five seconds; NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 falls back to 2000, delaying timeout completion by two seconds.

findings.title: Preserve zero-duration runner settings
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed `> 0` guard now replaces an explicit `"0"` configuration with the fallback. The resulting duration is used for the post-timeout SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL delay and SIGKILL give-up delay, so deployments relying on immediate escalation now wait 5000 ms or 2000 ms.

findings.title: Allow zero-duration overrides
findings.whyItBreaks: An explicit value of "0" previously produced a 0 ms duration; it now falls back silently. Consequently, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 becomes 5000 ms rather than immediately escalating SIGTERM to SIGKILL, and NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 becomes 2000 ms rather than immediately stopping the wait. This is a backward-incompatible configuration regression.

findings.title: Restore review coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: Large reviews select at most six hotspots, but no longer create a tail hotspot for changed files omitted by the map result or by that limit. An 11-file PR whose map produces seven single-file hotspots deep-reviews only six files and can return a clean verdict without inspecting the seventh.

findings.title: Preserve blocking residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: A deep review can report a blocking residual risk when it cannot reach a safe verdict, but this code replaces all such results with an empty array before the critic and final verdict see them. The exported review path can therefore report no residual risk for a large PR that a deep pass explicitly marked as blocked.

findings.title: Keep distinct findings with matching title prefixes
findings.whyItBreaks: The deduplication key now omits whyItBreaks and truncates titles to 60 characters. Two independent findings on the same file, line, and category with equal title prefixes are merged, so one concrete defect is removed from the final review.

findings.title: Restore coverage for unselected changed files
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed code caps deep review at six hotspots and removes the former tail-coverage hotspot. For a large bundle whose mapper returns more than six disjoint hotspots, files only in later hotspots are never deep-reviewed, allowing the critic to approve changes that received no deep pass.

findings.title: Propagate blocking residual risks to the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep review can return a blocking residual risk, but the changed candidateMerged object replaces all residual risks with an empty array before it is serialized into the critic prompt. The critic therefore cannot preserve that unresolved evidence, and the final deriveVerdict call receives only the critic's output.

findings.title: Preserve residual risks from deep reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: Each deep pass can return a blocking residual risk, but candidateMerged replaces all of them with an empty array. The critic at src/core/review.ts:116 therefore cannot receive unresolved deep-review evidence, and its result alone is passed to deriveVerdict at src/core/review.ts:122.

findings.title: Deep-review changed files excluded by the hotspot limit
findings.whyItBreaks: The selected hotspot list is capped at six, and the deleted coverage backstop no longer adds changed files absent from those selections. When the map pass yields more than six hotspots, files represented only by later hotspots are not deep-reviewed and no residual risk records the incomplete coverage.

findings.title: Preserve focus and deep options for large reviews
findings.whyItBreaks: For large bundles, review() routes to reviewLarge() (src/core/review.ts:163-164). The changed map payload at src/core/review.ts:83-89 no longer includes bundle.focus or bundle.deep, and the changed deep prompt at src/core/review.ts:117-121 no longer substitutes bundle.focus. Large reviews therefore stop conveying caller-requested review scope/depth to their prompts, while reviewSmall() still serializes the complete Bundle.

findings.title: Keep forwarding focus to large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed large-review path removes focus from both the map bundle and each deep-review prompt. A nonempty focus request remains serialized by reviewSmall but is discarded when review selects reviewLarge, so large-review results no longer honor the requested scope or priority.

findings.title: Preserve focus when building large-review prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed map bundle no longer includes `bundle.focus`, and the deep prompt no longer substitutes `{{FOCUS}}`. Consequently, large-review map and deep passes lose a caller-supplied review focus while `reviewSmall` still serializes the complete bundle.

findings.title: Normalize rounded seconds into the next minute
findings.whyItBreaks: For values that round up at a minute boundary, the minute count is calculated before rounding seconds. For example, 119500ms now renders as `1m 60s` instead of the normalized `2m 0s`; 59500ms renders as `60s` rather than `1m 0s`.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 59,500–59,999 ms, `minutes` is 0 while `seconds` rounds to 60, rendering `60s` instead of `1m 0s`; for 119,500–119,999 ms it renders `1m 60s`. The previous total-second calculation correctly carried this boundary.

findings.title: Carry rounded seconds into minutes
findings.whyItBreaks: For 59,600 ms, minutes is computed as 0 before the remainder rounds to 60, so rendered stats show "60s" instead of "1m 0s". Values such as 119,600 ms similarly render as "1m 60s".

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed comparison permits `parsePositiveInteger("0", label)` to return 0, while this exported API and its thrown-error message promise a positive integer. Callers relying on that contract can receive zero instead of a validation error.

findings.title: Reject zero in parsePositiveInteger
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed predicate accepts "0" and returns 0, while the exported function name and its thrown-error contract promise a positive integer. Public callers can therefore receive a value that violates the documented positive (>0) constraint.

findings.title: Reject zero in the positive-integer parser
findings.whyItBreaks: The changed condition accepts input "0" and returns 0, while the exported function name and its thrown error both promise a positive integer. Public callers can therefore receive a value outside the documented domain.
